They have broken down; they are practically all hamstrung to-day, and in bad financial condition. Their champions, and they have several, have said in the prominent American newspapers and magazines in the last few weeks that the only salvation for the American railroads lies in their electrification, and, that before that can be done the two hundred company-owned lines in the United States must be consolidated into ten or twelve systems. If that is done, and the railways are electrified, there may be some hope for the American roads, and still more hope if the magnificent waterways we have in connection with the St. Lawrence are developed for the transportation of steamships and for the generation of power.
There is one man in Canada who, like Joseph in Egypt, saw what was coming. Joseph had divine inspiration behind him, but there is a man in Canada to-day who had the foresight of Joseph, and who saw that the development of electrical energy was to be his main mission in life, and Sir Adam Beck to-day has this to his credit: He is the one man who foresaw what was coming, and he had the hardihood-and it is said to be a crime that he is guilty of- to see that the great development of waterpower energy by the public would go a long way toward the settlement of the transportation problem. And Adam Beck has this further achievement to his credit, that he has the greatest public development of water-power in the world at Chippawa and Niagara. It is a fine example of a publicly-owned transportation system operated by electrical energy, owned by the people, and a system the purpose of which is not primarily to make profits, but to give service.
Who has brought that about? It is not
private companies that have made this great demonstration to the world. The municipalities of Ontario have given this example, and up to date they have not lost a dollar in this connection. People say: "Adam Beck has made this and that mistake; he has exceeded his estimate," and his great critic is the Drury government. But when a government begins to criticise another organization for extravagance or carelessness, let me ask how their estimates compare with those of Sir Adam Beck? He has kept well within his estimates and he has made good. The people who are behind him have not lost a cent, and there has not been any graft in connection with the development of this power. The power is there; the exhibition of it is there, and you can see it every day now. Let the new Minister of Railways start to electrify the railways at once with all the power that he can get from the Ontario system, and let him begin to move cars from Niagara to the Detroit river, and from Niagara through Toronto where most of the traffic is. We have there two great National roads, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern. We can also sell some electrical power to the Canadian Pacific if they want it. I believe the Canadian Pacific are willing to buy power; they are simply waiting to buy power for the electrification of their railways. They hope to buy it from companies in Montreal, and I should like to see them get it there; but no matter who gets the power, the Government must take control of the electrification of railways and must fix the price.
I have almost finished my remarks, but I come back to the same statement I made the other day in regard to transportation. I have been in this House long enough to see freight rates reduced time after time by the Railway Commission that we established in this country, and every time a dollar was taken off railway freight rates in the moving of our crops, that dollar was put on by the steamship ring that controls transportation on the Atlantic. That cannot be done when the people own the transportation facilities, and therein lies the protection of the public. When the government of the United States-and this is what private transportation companies are afraid of-join, as I hope they will gladly join, with the present Government in developing electrical energy on the St. Lawrence river right in front of us and in two or three other places where power can be generated, we shall have the railway companies of the United States and of Canada in the hands of the people. This will give

Electrification

us a better lever for controlling freight rates than any commission or anything of the kind. We will furnish power to move your trains, provided you make the freight rates reasonable. There is the real problem of transportation in this country, and the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslau-riers) pointed it out to-night. I have studied this problem, and I hope we shall hear more to-night in favour of electrification of the railways of Canada, based on public control, and best of all, if it can be effected, based on public ownership of the sources of electrical energy. If we have that, we shall make real progress towards lower freight charges in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it my duty to speak to the resolution moved by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers). This question may be viewed from many angles. I think the whole House has been well informed about the matter from a technical point of view; but the question may be looked at from the point of view of 'local interests. For instance, every hon. member knows my constituency, Westmount-St. Henri, which is divided into two big portions, one on the upper level, namely, Westmount, and the other on the plains, the two wards of St. Henri and St. Cune-gonde. Hon. members who have travelled through the province of Quebec via the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern, or the Central Vermont, have passed through those centres, and they know how the population is suffering as a result of that traffic, and from the smoke which spoils everything, and is even injurious to human life.
This resolution must also be considered from a general point of view as far as public health and civic progress are concerned. In Montreal, there are electrical locomotives leaving the Canadian National railway station, and in all parts of the United States electrical locomotives are being used with great success. No doubt, the problem can be easily solved by the electrification of locomotives; the population, especially in urban centres, will not be inconvenienced by the dense smoke, and great benefit will ensue in connection with public health and child welfare if this resolution is adopted by the House.
I understand that the Government is obliged to say that it is shouldering very large expenses; but if this discussion has the result of inducing the Government to do its utmost to remedy the situation, the

populations of the large urban centres will benefit thereby. I remember reading that Max Hopkins used to say, when he was looking at a locomotive, "I take off my hat to it." If fuel locomotives are replaced by electrical locomotives when trains are passing through cities, the people will continue to practise that maxim by raising their hats to this new electrification of progress.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. C. KENNEDY (Minister of Railways) :
speechtext:
The thanks of the House are due to the member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers) ler bringing this resolution to its attention. He has displayed a keen interest in the question of the electrification of our railroads, which is one of great moment to the people of the country. The member for South York (Mr. Maclean) also made an interesting contribution to the debate, although, perhaps, he discussed the matter from a different angle from that of my hon. friend from Montreal. Those of us who come from Ontario, however, and who know that the hon. member for South York was one of the pioneers in the advocacy of the electrical development of our railways, and all that goes to make for the successful development of eletrical energy in our province, feel sure that those who have the matter in charge will give the hon. member's views every consideration. I have taken this matter up with the Board of Directors and the Board of Management of the Railways, who are keenly alive to the situation and know what is being done not only in this country but also on the other side. They are aware that the New York Central, the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway, and many other roads on the other side, use electrical energy, but they feel that in Canada the change at present would entail a very large expenditure, which the result of investigations that have been made is hardly conclusive enough to warrant. It is considered, therefore, that it would be better, for the present at any rate, ro defer action in the matter. Probably all that my hon. friend from St. Mary had in mind was just to bring the matter to the attention of Parliament, and I know that he will feel satisfied when I tell him that everything in connection with the development of electrical energy is being closely watched by the Board of Management of the Railways. They are not only interested in the question, but are also sympathetic, and when the right time comes they will do their part. In the meantime I would suggest to my hon. friend, if it meets with his approval, now that we have

Military Service Act
had a discussion of the subject, that he withdraw his resolution.
Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member have leave to withdraw the resolution?
Carried.

I might direct the attention of the House to the fact that, at first sight, the resolution does not seem to be in order. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should take steps to electrify the Canadian Government railways on all lines where electric power is available.
Reading it a second time, however, I find that it contains only a pious wish, on the part of the hon. member who moves it, that the Government should take certain action in respect to the matter he brings before the House. The hon. member invites the Government to make an investigation; that, undoubtedly, is what is meant by "taking steps." Section 54 of the British North America Act reads:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill, for the Appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any Tax or Impost, to any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the Governor General in the session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill is proposed.
I must remind hon. members on both sides of the House that when a resolution is adopted it is binding on the Government; and any resolution that calls for the expenditure of public moneys must originate with the Government. In the present instance, the resolution is simply a request that the Government should investigate the matter in question. For that reason I have allowed the discussion, which otherwise would not have been in order.
Motion withdrawn.

Mr. JAMES S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg Centre) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to repeal the Military Service Act, 1917. He said:
I shall not say much on this motion. I take it that the Military Service Act was very fully discussed on almost every political platform in the country. I understand that it is a matter of legal dispute as to * whether or not the act is still operative or whether it became void automatically with the cessation of the war. If it is dead, it seems to me that the least we can do is to give it decent burial. The war has ended, and we are glad to think that the circumstances which may or may not have made necessary the passing of the Military Service Act no longer exist. I therefore ask that that act be repealed.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the Military Service Act were still in operation the Government would be only too glad to accept the hon. member's suggestion and repeal it. But the act has ceased for some time past to be operative, and there is therefore, in the opinion of the Government, no need for the proposed legislation. My hon. friend has said that it is a matter of legal dispute whether or not the act is still in force. I can, I think, give my hon. friend assurance on that point which will be satisfactory to him and to the House. I have the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, agreed to by the Parliamentary Counsel, Mr. Gisborne. There is no doubt whatever in the minds of authorities who advise the Government on legal matters, as to the exact position of this legislation. The opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice is as follows:
The Military Service Act, Chapter 19 of 1917, was passed, as the recitals show, for the single purpose of enabling the Government to embody, by selective draft, re-inforcements. not exceeding 100,000 men (section 13, subsection 4) "to maintain and support the Canadian Expeditionary Force now engaged in active service overseas". By section 4, sub-section 1, the Governor General in Council was authorized

Military Service Act
to call out by proclamation any of the classes of men described by the Act for service "for the duration of the present war and of demobilization thereafter." The Act plainly had its application only to the circumstances then existing, and in relation to the war then in progress. The Act is now exhausted and spent and could not be invoked for another emergency. Therefore it is not necessary to repeal it.
If the statutes were being revised, Mr. Speaker, the commissioners would simply drop this act altogether. For us to proceed any further would he to take action which is wholly unnecessary.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Of the correctness of the position taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) there is no doubt whatever. The act has no present force and effect; there is no room for legal dispute of any kind on that point. The act plainly applied to the then war, and to no other; it could not by any government be applied to any other emergency, contingency, or war whatsoever. Consequently, on the termination of that war, the act became obliterated so far as actual operation at any time is concerned. However, the fact that it applied to the one state of hostilities and to that alone did not prevent a very prolonged and bitter assault being made upon it in the late campaign, and I have no doubt many hon. members of this House count it among their pledges that they would repeal this law,-a law which already was repealed; a law which, if you can speak of it in that way, was functus offiicio-absolutely without power of operation. That was the plan adopted of attacking the method of selective conscription which that law embodied.
If, however, it is the purpose of the hon. member or of any other hon. member or of the Government to wipe conscription from our statute book, there is yet much to be done. The Militia Act contains a provision for conscription, for compulsory military service-not through selection by tribunals; not by selection of any kind, but merely by the casting of lots,-by chance. The Governor in Council is empowered under the Militia Act, as it is to-day and has been on our statutes for decades, to compel military service in this country or out of this country for the defence of Canada at any time the Governor in Council or Parliament deems such a course necessary. Consequently, the principle of compulsory military service is as much embedded in our law as the principle of compulsory financial service by way of taxation. If, therefore,

there are those pledged against it who desire to redeem their pledge-which, of course. I have grave reason to doubt, on this or any other subject-the course to be pursued would be to attack the Militia Act of this country. I for one will await with much interest, though with little apprehension, any attack that may be made upon it.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire only to correct a misapprehension on the part of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). He seems to be unaware of the campaign that was carried on in my province with regard to the Military Service Act at the last election. My right hon. friend says that there are men in this House who sit here, probably, because they took a pledge to have that act repealed. I wish to tell him that those who took that pledge were defeated at the last election, and they were the friends of my right hon. friend. We were opposed by the friends of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, mind you, because we were supposed to have supported conscription. We, they said, were those who had been in favour of conscription; and they attacked us because we did not ask the repeal of that act after the war was over. The position I took then, the position we on this side of the House took, was the position that has just been taken by my right hon. friend: that the Military Service Act is no longer in force and that these gentlemen, supporters of my right hon. friend were absolutely mistaken.
I will give my right hon. friend some further information. His colleagues, the new ministers who were appointed to represent the province of Quebec,-Dr. Normand, fellow citizen of my hon. friend to my right (Mr. Bureau); Mr. Monty, and the others-came down to the province of Quebec and said in their speeches that we were responsible for conscription; that if they had been in the House at the time they would have opposed it; that we were the conscriptionists and that the colleagues of my right hon. friend were those opposed to it. That was the campaign in the province of Quebec at the last election, and my right hon. friend is mistaken when he states otherwise.

Will my hon. friend permit me to ask again a favour I so often ask,-that is, that he support his assertions as to other people by quotation?

Military Service Act
Everyone knows that in my province; no one would deny it. All those who read newspapers, whether they live in the province of Quebec or elsewhere, know that what I say is correct.
I will support mine.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend
(Mr. Lapointe) does not, perhaps, know of the service rendered to me in Three Rivers at the last election by the leader of the official Opposition (Mr. Meighen). It was my privilege to have as my opponent the then President of the Privy Council. This gentleman came on the stump and asserted- and a list of the members in question was published in one of the papers supported by the friends of my right hon. friend- that those who voted for and supported conscription were the Liberals in Opposition in 1917. But I was saved in this way: My right hon. friend came to Three Rivers and said in the course of a speech there: "I am the father of conscription". I called a meeting and I asked the President of the Privy Council, who was right, he or his leader; and when he was caught between the two he did not answer. Thus the situation was saved.
Now, my right hon. friend wants quotations. If he will have patience and wait until to-morrow I will send him the newspapers of Three Rivers from which he will see that prior to his visit to that city there was not a speech made by the President of his Privy Council-and we had three or four meetings every evening in those days; it was a great fight-in which it was not stated that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the then Opposition, naming your humble servant as one of the members of it, were the fathers and promoters of conscription. But after my right hon. friend came to Three Rivers, they changed their tune. They said: "Well, conscription was not invented in 1917; it was instituted at the time of Confederation. Sir George Etienne Cartier was the father of conscription. Subsequently Sir Frederick Borden changed the act; it was he who imposed conscription upon the people; therefore, the law of 1917 was nothing new; we simply took your act and put it into force." Then we put the question, "Why did you change it if you already had authority to raise armies for overseas? Why didn't you use that law? Why did you pass a new one?" "Oh," they said, "the war was a new thing; the conditions were entirely new; everything was new." I make the
statement here that in the province of Quebec the fight was made, whether it was inspired by the leader of the Opposition or not, on the charge that the Opposition of that day, in 1917, were the people that brought about conscription. But when my right hon. friend went through the province saying that he was the father of conscription these people changed their minds and said, "So it dates from the consolidation of the Militia Act," and they were opposed to it and said: "The Militia Act will be wiped off the statute book. We as a self-respecting nation do not want that." My right hon. friend does not need to ask for quotations, because I could load him up with so many that it would take him the balance of the session to read them. So I will ask him to "dispense"; it will save him work and the country will be as well informed.

I should like to gratify the request of the leader of the Opposition for a quotation. I happen to have one in my pocket at the moment. During the recent campaign Mr. Belley the ex-Postmaster General, was the candidate of my right hon. friend in the county of Charlevoix-Mont-morency and I can quote from a speech he made as reported in the Quebec Chronicle, the owner of which was the late Sir David Watson, a well known friend of the Tory government and of the government that has just passed away. This is what that newspaper report says:
With documentary evidence in hand Mr. Belley proved that the Conscription Act was contained in the Laurier law,-
Hear, hear.

-as it appears in the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1906. The Borden Act did not change this Act, but simply changed the mode of raising troops. By the Laurier Act the troops were raised by lottery while the Borden Act provided for selection by exemption tribunals.
AM true.

By the lottery system enacted in the Laurier Act hundreds of young men would have gone to war, hut under the Borden exemption system not a single young man of Charlevoix county went to the war. But the point which impressed the audience most was the voting of five hundred million dollars which Mr. Borden had obtained in the session of 1918. He explained that the Borden Act was passed before the elections of 1917, the elections having been held in December that year. At the beginning of the session of 1918 Mr. Borden presented a hill bearing No. 38, by which he asked Parliament for a sum of five hundred million dollars which

Military Service Act

was required, amongst other things, for^ the enforcing of the Conscription Act. Not a single member had voted against the granting of this money, not even the Liberal members, who had taken pledges only a few months before that they would ask for the repeal of the Military Service Act.
Several members then sought Mr. Belley's permission to ask him a few questions, and he readily consented and answered all questions decisively.
I hope that quotation will satisfy my right hon. friend.
If I may be permitted a remark, I am thankful to my hon. friend for confirming precisely what I stated was the case.

My hon. friend from Quebec West (Mr. Parent) has just given the House a quotation from the Quebec Chronicle with reference to the campaign of the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Belley) in the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency. I happen to have been the fortunate candidate in that election. I succeeded in beating one of the ministers who had (enjoyed office for a few days under my right hon. friend who now leads the Opposition. Every word that has been quoted by my hon. friend from Quebec West is absolutely true. I could also quote to the House, if I wished to detain it, many more statements circulated in the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency at the expense of the people of this country to show that conscription was the work of the Liberal party. I answered each and every one of these statements on the platform, and with the aid of some of my friends, especially the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), I succeeded in obtaining the victory over one of the ministers of my right hon. friend opposite. The first statement which was published referred to the voting of $500*000,000; which !was required among other things for the enforcing of the Conscription Act. I answered that which was not absolutely correct, and several other statements that were made about conscription at that time. We did not raise the issue. It was the hon. gentlemen now sitting angularly opposite who raised it, although they accuse us of having raised the issue to get us back into power. I want to say publicly here in the House that if the election in the province of Quebec was carried on the conscription issue, it was not carried by the Liberal party, but by hon. gentlemen sitting angularly opposite from me here. I shall vote with pleasure for the repeal of this law.

Mr. Speaker, in my humble opinion this bill is useless. I agree with my hon. friend the Prime Minister that the law is not now in operation, and I only rise to answer in two words the right hon. ex-member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) who now sits angularly opposite by the grace, generosity, and skilful tactics of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I happen to have with me a few quotations that he challenged my hon. friend from Quebec East to produce T have a quotation, for instance, from a speech made by the ex-Seeretary of State, Mr. Monty, on conscription, as reported in La Minerve, a Montreal paper carrying on its front page the photograph of the leader of the official Opposition. I will translate from La Minerve of November 5th, 1921 as follows:
The Hon. Mr. Monty in Beauharnois
The Hon. Mr. Monty spoke afterwards on conscription. He declared that in 1917 he was opposed to that law. No one could doubt it. He had defended hundreds and hundreds of conscripts. He had adopted and he was still willing to defend the principle of Sir John A. Macdonald that Canada should have an army only for the defence of Canadian territory. He openly declared that if ever in future the same question came up he would oppose conscription and defend his anti-conscription principles. "You can say," repeated the Secretary of State ''that I was against conscription, that I am still against conscription, that I will be against conscription on the 6 th of December, that I always will be against conscription."
If this quotation is not sufficient I can read further extracts from a newspaper that was published in the constituency of Three Rivers, the St. Lawrence Valley Chronicle, quoting speeches delivered by the Hon. Dr. Normand. That gentleman, who was president of the Privy Council is reported as saying the following:
Conscription is not a matter of principle but simply a matter of contribution, and I said it and I repeat it again, and I always said during conscription time, that I was opposed to conscription, and I am still opposed to conscription. I thought it was a bad system of administration. I was also opposed to it because I considered it the wrong way and I am still opposed to it. In the present election there are Nationalists who state that we should never participate in the wars of the Empire. I am with those, I am somewhat of a Nationalist myself.
Dr. Normand also said that he had always opposed conscription which he condemned vigorously saying that on that question he agreed with the Nationalist idea on the subject. Now I will not further occupy the time of the House in reading these newspapers. I have probably

Military Service Act
ten or fifteen numbers of the paper La Minerve showing the whole fight in the province of Quebec carried on by the ex-ministers-the ministers pro tern as I might call them-was on this question. The Liberals did not bring on this issue in the province of Quebec. It was the friends of the leader of the Opposition.
Oh, no.
Hear, hear.

I can quote
from another copy of La Minerve a list conspicuously printed on the first page of Liberal members of the province of Quebec who were accused of having voted for the principle of conscription.

And I was one of
them.

The list sets forth the names of Messrs. Bureau, Brou-illard, Bickerdike, Boivin, Bourassa, Boyer, Cardin, Deslisle, Demers, Devlin, Ethier, Fortier and so on. That was the fight that was waged by friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in the province of Quebec in the last election. How different from the fight conducted in 1917 when the Liberals were accused of being friends of the Kaiser and not willing to do their duty in the war. I will not say anything further, but I am sure my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will not insist upon any more quotations, and will be a little more chary about issuing challenges in future.
I have never contended, and have never even said, that the ministers who came into the Government had been or were in favour of conscription.
But you took them into the Cabinet.
Was the question of the attitude of the ministers on conscription never discussed before their entrance into the Cabinet?

The bill proposes to repeal a statute which is no longer in effect, because it is exhausted. The Government takes that view and so does the leader of the Opposition. That is also the opinion of the law officers. Surely the war was concluded by the ratification of the three Treaties, Versailles, St. Germain and Sevres. There is nothing for us to discuss here, so why bring such a question before the House. The discussion will not advance the business of the House one iota. Its only effect is to transfer to this Chamber-for a motive I am unable to appreciate-a debate which will have not the slightest effect upon the members of this House, whatever influence it might have if conducted from the hustings.
Mr. HENRI E. LAVIGUEUR (Quebec County): When conducting the fight in my constituency at the last election I had to face opponents who demanded of me that I should ask Parliament, if circumstances permit, to repeal the Conscription Act. At that time I happened to have as my opponent Mr., Armand Lavergne, the chief of the Nationalist party in the district of Quebec. That gentleman opposed me on the ground that I had not asked Parliament to repeal the act of 1917. Mr. Lavergne was supported in that fight by chiefs of the Conservative party, some of whom were the intimate friends of the leader of the Opposition. I told the electors at the time exactly what the hon. member who has just taken his seat has stated to the House 

that the Conscription Act was dead and that there was no need to repeal a dead law. Now I am happy to have the statement I made at that time confirmed in this House by no less a person than the leader of the Opposition himself.
Mr. H. A. FORTIER (Labelle), (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, I have but a few remarks to add with reference to the proposed legislation which is before this House. I do not wish to recall the unpleasant reminiscences of the last general election. The electors of the county of Labelle returned me with such a large majority that I can afford, in this instance, to be magnanimous and not take any notice of the declarations made by my opponents. I then declared in the presence of my electors that there was no necessity of a special bill for the repeal of the Military Service Act as the latter did not exist. These declarations, I believe, are absolutely identical to those made in this House by the hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King), and moreover by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I still hold to this opinion as I contended before my electors, that no necessity exists to bring in a special bill for the repeal of the Conscription Act. However, seeing that the Prime Minister has given us communication of a letter of the legal adviser to the Justice Department, leading to the belief
National Defence

that perhaps in certain parts of the country, there seems to exist doubts on the advisability of such a bill, I emphatically declare that I am in favour of this bill, if its mover persists in submitting it to the consideration of this House. I have always been opposed to conscription, and if the measure is necessary, I shall gladly give my support to a bill which would repeal the Military Service Act of 1917.

In my judgment this-discussion is out of order. Any resolution presented in the House must have something positive as to its effect. If a motion is made or a bill introduced with a view to repeal legislation, that legislation must be in existence. From the opinions of the Law Officers of the House of Commons and of the Deputy Minister of Justice, and, after the opinion expressed by some of the leaders on both sides, I come to the conclusion that the Military Service Act, 1917, cannot be repealed, because it has exhausted itself, and is considered as non-existent at present in the statutes. Therefore I give it as my opinion that this bill should be dropped and that the discussion should not proceed and I so rule.

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence) moved that the House to-morrow go into Committee of the Whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved-1. That it is expedient to bring in a measure to create a department of the Government of Canada to be called the Department of National Defence, over which a Minister of the Crown shall preside who shall be the Minister of National Defence.
2.	That the Minister shall be charged with all matters relating to Defence, including the Militia, the Military, Naval, Air and Police Services of Canada.
3.	That there shall be a Deputy Minister of National Defence who shall be appointed by the Governor in Council, and hold office during pleasure, and such officers may be appointed as are necessary for the carrying on of the business of the department.
4.	That the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister may appoint an officer who shall, in relation to the Naval Service exercise all the powers and duties vested in the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service by or under The Naval Service Act, and who shall have the rank and salary of a Deputy Head of a department, and shall be a member of the Defence Council.
5.	That the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister may appoint an officer to be known as Comptroller, who under the Deputy Minister of National Defence, shall be charged with all financial matters pertaining to the Department of National Defence.
TMr. Fortier ]
6.	That any person whose position is abolished on the coming into force of the Act to be based upon these Resolutions may, on the recommendation of the Minister, be appointed by the Governor in Council to such position in the Department and with such rank, title and salary as shall be prescribed.
7.	That if any person is removed from office or an appointment in consequence of the abolition of his office or his appointment by the Act based upon these Resolutions or by any order or regulation thereunder, or is retired within two years after the coming into force of the said Act, the Governor in Council may grant him a gratuity, retiring or superannuation allowance, or pension not exceeding such as he would have been entitled or eligible to receive if he had been retired under the provisions of any Act applicable to him, after adding from one to three years, as the Governor in Council may deem advisable, to his actual term of service.
8. 9. I think it would be opportune now if the Minister of Agriculture would give us an explanation of an appointment which has been made in his department to a post that it had not been considered necessary to fill for some time, and the making of which, so far as any information I have goes, was wholly against the provision, the spirit, if not, indeed, the letter of the Civil Service Act. I refer to the appointment of Mr. Duncan Marshall to the position of Commissioner of Agriculture. The Civil Service Commission classified this position and1 fixed the maximum salary, I think, at $4,200. Even with the classification there, owing to the fact that the Agricultural Instruction Act had got wholly under way, there was no very great difficulty to Ibe encountered in the completion of the grants to be -made under that act. It was not considered necessary to fill the position and incur that expenditure, because the officers of the department felt themselves wholly capable of taking care of all the work that had been done previously by the commissioner. Notwithstanding this the present Government has appointed a Commissioner of Agriculture, and as the reports state-and I do not think it is disputed-has repealed the Civil1 Service recommendation as to salary, and gone beyond the maximum by about $1,800 to commence with, giving Mr. Marshall $6,000 a year at the public expense. I believe that in relation to certain subjects in his department we have had the spectacle lately of the deputy minister- who by the way draws only $6,000 himself- having an officer under him drawing the same salary. I do not know whether the minister counts the Commissioner of Agriculture under the deputy minister or not. Possibly there are two executive heads in his department. We have had the spectacle of these two officers giving diametrically opposite statements as to matters affecting the department in relation to the embargo. I think the House is entitled to an explanation as to why they saw fit to fasten this charge on the public, and whether or not it was on the recommendation of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, a most efficient officer.

This is a matter that does not come under the head of civil government as Mr. Mashall's salary is dealt with in the estimate for the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, however, I wall be very pleased to give the explanation.
How does the minister justify taking an officer's salary, which is a civil government matter, out of civil government, and putting it under the other estimate?

Mr. Duncan
Marshall has not been appointed Commissioner of Agriculture at all.
What position has he been appointed to?

If I have the permission of the Chair, I will read the Order in Council, and probably that will speak for itself. I may say that I think answers to questions in regard to this matter were tabled to-day: This is the Order in Council:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 1st February, 1922, from the Minister of Agriculture, submitting that the Agricultural Instruction Act under which the suih of $1,100,000 annually has been granted to the Provincial Departments of Agriculture for the purpose of aiding agricultural instruction in the provinces expires March 31st, 1923.
The minister states that in view of the extraordinary and exceptional conditions in the agricultural world it is highly desirable that an investigation be made into the advisability of the continuation, discontinuation or emendation of the provisions of this Act; the amounts to be paid, and the methods of calculating such amounts in the event of its. extension; and the scope of the work of the provinces to be undertaken- with the assistance of funds provided thereunder.
It is considered advisable that a commissioner be appointed under section 38c of the Civil Service Act as amended by chapter 22 of the Statutes of 1921, to conduct the investigation indicated above, and to inquire into such other agricultural problems as may be desirable and necessary.
The minister, therefore recommends that Mr. Duncan Marshall, of Olds, Alberta, be appointed as a commissioner for the above purpose, and to perform such other duties of a cognate nature as may be delegated to him.
The minister further recommends that Mr. Marshall be paid a salary at the rate of $6,000 per annum, said salary to be paid from the appropriation provided for the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act and that this appointment date from January 15, 1922.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
I will read simply that part of section 38a:, beginning within five lines of the bottom, which has to do more particularly with the subject under consideration:
Nothing in this Act shall affect the powers of the Governor in Council with respeot to the appointment of any commissioner or other member of any Hoyal or other commission or board, or any deputy head.

The appointment was made under that section, not as Commissioner of Agriculture, but as a commissioner to make certain investigations with respect to the continuance, or non-continuance or amendment of the Agricultural Instruction Act. That is what he is engaged in doing now, and I hope we shall have his report in time to determine what will be the character of the legislation. The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), in his speech on the Address, referred to the absence of any reference to this. We are contemplating bringing down legislation; but before doing so, we shall have the special report stating how this legislation can be improved or extended, or whether it should be left just the way it is.
Am I to gather from my hon. friend's remarks that this question is not a permanent one?
It is a temporary appointment.
How long is it expected to last?
About six months, probably. .

The minister of course, could not help noticing, as he read the Order in Council, that the duties assigned to Mr. Marshall are just the duties that would be performed by the Commissioner of the Agricultural Education Branch, were he appointed to fill that office for which the Civil Service Commission fixes a salary of 54,200 a year only. Did Mr. Marshall, as part of his duties in this office, make a trip to Mexico recently?
He has not been here for two or three weeks.
Was the trip to Mexico a part of the investigation into the Agricultural Education Branch?
No.

Was it a trip at the
public expense?
So far as I know, he did not go to Mexico.
Was it Florida? Was his trip there part of his duties under the Order in Council?

That was not
amongst his duties enumerated in the Order in Council.

Did he take that trip
as a public official, or was it a private job?

When the right
hon. gentleman has finished, I will endeavour to answer his question.

That is the first question. The next is this. Surely the minister does not contend that that section of the Civil Service Act can be utilized merely by giving a man another name as an excuse for giving him another salary.

With respect to
Mr. Marshall's duties, apart from the investigation into the working of the Agricultural Instruction Act, I may say that he is conducting an investigation with respect to the exhibition grant throughout Canada. As my right hon. friend knows, in the past about $180,000 have been paid by the Dominion Department of Agriculture by way of exhibition grants. That seems a large sum of money, and he is conducting a special inquiry as to how much those grants can be reduced without materially affecting the success of those exhibitions. Another matter is the question of the working out of the "accredited herd" policy of the present Government. This work is being taken up with great vigour; the amount of money set aside in the past for it has not been sufficient to meet the situation, and certain amendments are under consideration. I might point out that no herds under twelve in number have been inspected, and the result has been that complaints have been made about discrimination in favour of the man with the big herd, inasmuch as the man with the small herd does not come within the scope of the act. When Mr. Marshall comes back and completes his report with respect to these matters, as I hope he will be able to do in the course of two or three weeks, we have under consideration sending him to some South American countries, either Argentine, or Brazil, or Chili, or probably them all, this matter depending on the information which we get from the Department of Trade and Commerce as to which of these countries will prove, at the present time, the best market for our pure-bred herds that just now have difficulty in finding a market. As my right hon. friend and the committee know, the foot-and-mouth disease, that is so prevalent in the old country at this time, makes it impossible for any of these countries to get their breeding animals from the usual source in the United Kingdom. It was, therefore, thought that this would be a good time to set up a market for our pure-bred animals in these countries, and that we might possibly be able to continue it. Their business relations with Canada

Supply-Agriculture
are good at the present time, and as they are not able to get pure-bred animals from the United Kingdom, we thought it would be a fortunate time to send one or two representatives of this department to these South American countries with the object that I have stated in view. Mr. Duncan Marshall, when he returns, with probably another gentleman, Mr. Dryden, will be delegated, if the information we get from the Department of Trade and Commerce justifies us in sending them, to these South American countries to open up a market more particularly for pure-bred animals.

What was his last
trip in connection with?

With regard to
Florida, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and I sometimes exchange the work of our men. If the right hon. gentleman had been in the Chamber on Friday evening, he would have heard how we lent some of our entomologists to the Interior Department. Some of them went out in scouting parties and in aeroplanes to guide the lumbermen in directing their operations and in taking care of their lumber areas that are menaced by the spruce bud worm. There was a large exhibition in Florida, where the Department of the Interior was represented by Mr. Marshall, who did some work in connection with immigration.

I should like the minister to take a note and, when he hears of any immigrant coming from that district, let me know. Evidently Mr. Marshall is in for a good time. I believe Chili comes next, then the Bermudas, and so on. Will that expedition to Chili be for immigration, or in the interests of pure bred stock?
I thought I made that plain.

The South American trips would be in the interest of the Department of Agriculture. I am afraifl that six months will go by without much study into the question of the continuance of agricultural grants.

I am sorry if my right hon. friend has never heard of the prospects of the live stock markets in the Argentine, in Chili or in Patagonia. There is an exceedingly good prospect there for pure bred animals, especially as they are not available in Great Britain, where they were formerly got.

Is not that the work of the trade commissioners? If the trade
commissioners are not good enough, would it not be better to have Mr. Marshall appointed under the Department of Trade and Commerce and be paid a salary for this sort of work?
You could do it that way, but inasmuch as Messrs. Marshall and Dryden are both practical, first class live stock men, it was thought that they would be as successful as anyone else.
The salary limit was pretty low under the Civil Service Commission. That question came up too, I suppose.

I think it is quite well understood that some of the countries that have been mentioned-the Argentine and Chili-are already in the market for Canadian pure bred stock. They have already purchased our stock. Why have the Commissioner of Agriculture and Mr. Dryden been selected to form the committee? It is well known that both of these gentlemen are competent and are zealous in looking after the interests of beef breeds of cattle; but why have not the dairy interests 'been considered? It is dairy cattle that have been going to Chili and to the Argentine, and I cannot see why there should not be some one to represent the dairy breeds, which, I think we all agree, are quite as important in Canada as the beef breeds.

Neither Mr. Marshall nor Mr. Dryden is unfamiliar with the dairy interests. It is true that they have paid more attention to 'beef cattle, but in regard to any one whom we might appoint the question might be asked: Why not appoint some one else? Judging from the nature of questions on the Order Paper, one might be inclined to think that it was something different that some hon. members had in view. The question is asked, for instance: Was one of these gentlemen a defeated candidate? I do not see that that has anything to do with this subject. If any hon. gentleman thinks it has, let him ask the question.

Is not Mr. Duncan Marshall himself a large grower of beef cattle, and will he be prohibited from doing business on his own acount while travelling as a representative of the Goverment. He might have an eye for the main chance, and the minister might say whether there will be an express prohibition against his doing business in his own behalf.

I understand from the newspaper reports that Mr. Marshall has sold out his 'live stock and has rented his place. He is therefore completely at liberty to represent the Government. I do not know what his future plans may he, but I learn from the newspapers that he has disposed of his stock.

I endorse what my hon. friend (Mr. Brethen) has said with regard to the necessity for including an expert dairyman in the delegation which is going to South America to secure more trade for Canadian 'breeders of cattle. While both the gentlemen mentioned are well known and of great ability, we must remember that they have both specialised of late years in the beef cattle industry. It is well known that our dairy herds have been developed to a very high point indeed. In fact, we are producing certain specimens of dairy breeds that are among the very best in the world. We also know that there is a tremendous development of the dairy industry in South America, particularly in the Argentine. That country has been making very rapid strides of late years in the production of dairy breeds, and their products are shipped to Great Britain in competition with our own. I think therefore that the minister would be well advised if, in that delegation, he included an expert dairyman to explain to the people of the Argentine the benefits to be derived from the importation of Canadian dairy breeds. I am greatly interested in what the minister has to say with regard to the accredited herd system. This system is costing a great deal of money, but I think that it is accomplishing considerable good in Canada in eradicating tuberculosis from our herds. As we all know, tuberculosis has been making alarming progress, affecting not only cattle but hogs, and this is shown in our abattoir inspections. In the past the accredited herd system has been conducted largely through the minister, the deputy minister and the veterinary director general. I do not quite appreciate the reason for appointing a man, who is not a veterinarian, for the purpose of reporting upon this kind of work. I used to think that the old combination worked well indeed, and if there was any fault to be found with it, it was the barrier that we encountered when we went to the Minister of Finance for further assistance. The old combination worked well enough, and I do not think it is necessary to make any change now. Is 
it the intention to renew the fund, under the Agricultural Instruction Act, which will run out at an early date; and, will approximately the same sum of money be appropriated for the purpose for which that fund was provided? Does the Government intend to disburse that money in the way it has been spent during the past ten years, namely, by the provinces with a slight control exercised by the federal authorities? I should like to know also if the expenditure for agricultural grants for fairs has been cut down this year. These grants have done a great deal of good in developing exhibitions throughout the country, and I do not think that there is any particular agency that has rendered a greater service to the pure bred live stock business *of Canada and the cattle industry generally than the encouragement of these exhibitions. The reduction in grants will not .be felt to any great extent by the larger exhibitions, but the smaller and medium *sized fairs that obtain grants from the department will suffer considerably as a .result of a cut, I understand, of 50 per cent now under contemplation. On behalf of the exhibitions throughout the country *from coast to coast, I would ask the .minister to consider this point carefully *and try to make the reduction less in the case of the smaller exhibitions than in the ,ease of the larger ones that will not feel the reduction to the same extent. By following such a course he would let down the smaller exhibitions gently, so to speak, and would not interfere unduly with the work that they have carried on. The plans for these exhibitions are prepared in most cases, about a year in advance, and if a severe cut in their grant is made without warning, they may be involved in serious difficulties, particularly if bad weather is encountered and the gate receipts are much smaller than in former years.
Was it through Mr. Marshall's recommendation that the reduction in these grants was made?

Should Mr. Marshall's report indicate that injustice is being done to these exhibitions, the matter may be considered as reopened. I understood when we decided on the reduction of these grants that all the exhibition managers had been notified of the intended reductions from six months to a year ago. There is some doubt, however, about the accuracy of my information in that respect, and should Mr. Marshall's report indicate that hardship would follow as a

result of these cuts, there will be an opportunity of reconsidering the matter when we come to the vote in the Supplementary Estimates. In the Finance Minister's absence, of course, I do not want to say anything about the Supplementary Estimates that will startle him, but at least the matter can be considered. The member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) knows as well as I do that large sums of money have been handed out to exhibitions all over Canada during the last three or four years. There is no use in talking economy about a $2,000 civil servant, and then handing out $180,000 to these big exhibitions. There is no sense in that sort of thing. We have a certain amount for agriculture; what is the best way to spend it? Do we get as much value out of this expenditure as we would get out of $180,000 spent for other purposes. That is what we have to determine. In my opinion we get less value from the money granted to these exhibitions than we do from any other expenditure that is made in the Department of Agriculture. If we made the grant the same as before, I am sure my secretaries and stenographers would be saved a good deal of trouble in answering telegrams and inquiries of all kinds; but in my judgment a substantial reduction is justified. As I have intimated, however, if it is found that the exhibition- managers did not get proper notice, as I understod they did a year ago, the matter will be looked into, and possibly we might make the reduction only twenty per cent this year, with a further cut next year.
Another very proper question was put to me by the hon. gentleman who was my very capable predecessor-and I want to pay tribute to him; I found the department particularly the live stock branch, in excellent shape when I took office, and consider myself fortunate in being able to step into it. Now the hon. gentleman asked why Mr. Marshall interfered-I am not sure that is the word he used-with the accredited herds. That is a matter which has been left largely to the veterinarians. Only those who have had their animals tested and found to their dismay that they were affected with tuberculosis and had to be destroyed, know what it feels like. There is a good deal of feeling throughout the country that the tuberculin test is not the last word with respect to the diagnosis and treatment of this disease, and the view prevails that there ought to be some representation of the
man whose herds are proposed to be slaughtered. Both Duncan Marshall and myself know what it is, experimentally, to have one's herds slaughtered on account of tuberculosis, and there is no doubt that' those who own the cattle should be represented in such an important matter,

not merely the veterinarians, much as I may think of them. I may say in this connection that investigations are being made in Europe with a view to discovering some serum or vaccine or antitoxin that will take care of this disease by immunizing the animals when they are young, just as is done in the case of blackleg. If you could not treat blackleg when the animals are young, the mortality would be much greater than it is. Some progress has been made in that investigation. It is not one of the matters that I intended to have Duncan Marshall deal with, but what I do want him to get at is the viewpoint of the man who owns the herds. There is another point in this connection: the man who has only three or four head of cattle who is exempted from the operations of the accredited herd regulations wants to know why the big man should have access to this accredited herd money while he has not. These are some of the reasons why we want this matter inquired into, and I do not know any better man to do it than Duncan Marshall. He is himself a stock raiser; he has had his herds infected by tuberculosis, and has been co-operating with the federal Department of Agriculture in the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act.

What exhibitions are
qualified to receive the federal grant, and on what grounds are they so qualified?

I cannot have my whole staff here to deal with these various matters; this is the result of our getting away from the civil government estimates and into the matter of exhibitions. However, I can tell my hon. friend offhand that in Saskatchewan seven cities and towns receive grants from the federal treasury, amounting to almost a fabulous sum. As to Ontario, the city of Ottawa, for instance, gets a grant. I read in one of the morning papers the other day that the Ottawa fair had a surplus of $10,000 as a result of last year's operations, and that another exhibition had a surplus of $14,000. In the West, large salaries are being paid to the managers of exhibitions, in some cases as much as $10,000 a year, where large grants are given by the Do-

Supply-A griculture
minion as well as by the province. These $10,000 salaries are somewhat large compared with Mr. Marshall's modest $6,000, and in view of the surpluses which these ' exhibitions have in many cases it seems to me that with the exchequer in its present condition, a continuance of the usual large grants would be a little too prodigal.
Can my hon. friend give me the qualifications which entitle these exhibitions to grants?
If this matter comes up under another item, why should we discuss it under the civil government?

I have here the
statement of conditions under which grants were made to summer and fall exhibitions for the year 1922. There would be very little change this year. I might quote a few paragraphs:
Exhibition Associations whose shows are open In all live stock classes to the whole of the Dominion of Canada, will receive grants under the following conditions on the basis of the expenditure in prize money in the utility classes of live stock and poultry at their last exhibition :-
1.	Fairs, which have expended at their last preceding exhibition a minimum of $4,000.00 and up to $16,000.00 of a maximum of their own money for prizes in these classes and which have not received a grant from the Dominion Department of Agriculture for the show at which this expenditure was made, shall receive the minimum grant of $1,250.00.
2.	Such fairs as have not received a grant for their previous exhibition shall be entitled, in addition to the minimum grant as stated above, to a grant of 50 per cent of the expenditure over $4,000.00. The maximum grant, in no case, shall exceed $2,500.00.
3.	Fairs, which shall have expended at their last preceding show a minimum of $4,000.00 and up to $16,000.00 of a maximum of their own money for prizes in these classes plus the amount of the grant received from the Department for their preceding show, shall be entitled to the minimum grant of $1,250.00.
I take the ground that we should not let them down too suddenly. They went up gradually, and we should try and arrange it so as to give the least jolt to those concerned. The matter will undoubtedly be reconsidered later on when the report of Duncan Marshall comes in, as well as that of Dr. Grisdale, who has just returned from the West.

I have complete faith in
the Minister of Agriculture spending the moneys that are voted in a proper manner. I see that the staff contains from forty-eight to fifty new members, but hon. members will remember that in the discussions concerning agriculture in this House I have

always expressed the belief that the Department of Agriculture was nearer the paint of starvation than any other department of the Government.
With regard to this vaccine or antitoxin, I am sure that we should approve of the expenditure. A good many members of this House will recall along with myself that there was a time in the West when our stock was not inspected, and the thought came to me as the minister was speaking of a visit he himself had from an inspector who destroyed a certain portion of his herd on the ground that they were infected with tuberculosis. I remember once an inspector came on my farm and shot horses that were supposed to be suffering from glanders. He was receiving five dollars per head for every horse that he found infected with the disease, so naturally enough he was successful in finding a goodly number roundabout that were infected. I mention this in order to emphasize that the Department of Agriculture should be provided with sufficient money to provide for proper officers, so that we shall not be subjected in the future to enormities such as those I have described. I do not think the House is really opposed to voting this money. In past years, owners have suffered materially in Canada because of the ravages of various diseases among their stock, and those diseases are becoming even more prevalent in the herds of Canada to-day.

Speaking of the grants
for these agricultural exhibitions, while some of them may have reached a point where they are beyond the need of assistance, it must be remembered that though we have in western Canada five or six of the best fairs on this continent, they had to be built up by assistance from both federal and provincial governments, and without that assistance they would not have been the excellent shows they are to-day.
As far as the salaries are concerned, that is a matter for arrangement by the management of each exhibition. These exhibitions do not consist altogether of agriculture; manufacturers and many other lines are represented, although the grant is made on the ground that a certain sum of money has been paid for live stock at the exhibition of the previous year, so the ten thousand dollar salary paid to the manager of one of these western exhibitions is not only for his services as manager of the live stock, but for managing the whole show.
I was interested in what the minister had to say with regard to the accredited

Supply-Agriculture
herd system. He said that tuberculin, which is being used for the purpose of testing these cattle in the accredited herds, was not the last word in diagnosing tuberculosis. I claim that it is, so far as we know, and while we do not recognize tuberculin as an infallible agent, it is the very best we have including three tests for diagnosing tuberculosis. When we take into consideration our great loss from this disease, particularly in our abattoirs and in swine from dairy districts, I think the Government has been quite justified in the past in using the very best methods at hand for the eradication of this disease. There is a great deal to do in that direction in the future.
Wtih regard to the use of serums for immunizing, and so on- that has nothing whatever to do with the accredited herd system, but a system of experiment should be carried on along these lines whenever any agency is found that gives promise of combatting this great disease. But that has nothing to do with tuberculin as a diagnostic agent.

I would point out that it is not possible for the fairs in the West to get the attendance or the admission fees possible in the East with its heavier settlement, and consequently it is more necessary to give assistance to the western fairs. I have had experience enough to know that if these fairs are not given the grant this year, probably many of them will be spoilt. I think they should have, at the worst, at least one year's warning before the grant is withdrawn, because they have made their arrangements on the basis of receiving the grant. They could not possibly carry on with any fair amount of success with a very much lower grant from the Dominion Government.

There is a question I would like to ask the minister in connection with this vote and it is this: Considerable anxiety was expressed at one of our recent sittings by reason of the fact that insufficient encouragement is given to those who are deserving of promotion in the Civil Service. That being the case does the Minister of Agriculture consider it a desirable thing to give to an outsider like Mr. Duncan Marshall what the public would consider a plum in the Civil Service? Is this an encouragement to those who have worked so long and faithfully in the Civil Service?

My hon. friend has raised a very good point and it is one
I considered very carefully before I made my decision. The present Government, it must be remembered, has only been in power about three months. Now it was only at the beginning of the new year, or very shortly afterwards, that it was made apparent to me that the Agricultural Instruction Act would have to be dealt with at this session of Parliament. That information came to me quite unexpectedly and quite suddenly. My staff at that time were all busily engaged; there was a convention in progress at one end of Canada with regard to a particular topic, and another convention dealing with something else at the other end of the Dominion at which our officers were in attendance. Even at the present time a number of the staff are just returning from a live stock convention at Saskatoon; and we had not at the time I refer to a single man available to take up that particular line of investigation work. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) can testify if he likes that when he presided over this department the staff were all busy. They are always busy and particularly in the early months of the year. Here was the session coming on, and we wanted to deal with this question in a thorough and intelligent way; we wanted to ascertain just what the facts were. Very well, how are you going to get facts unless you send out a representative to procure them? Take my position to-night. I am without proper assistance owing to the absence of the deputy minister. It is quite true that on the civil government estimates the official who is here advising me is as good an authority as I could get; but in the matter of experimental farms and exhibitions Dr. Grisdale is the best authority available because he has been so closely identified with them. Now then, so far as the qualifications of Mr. Duncan Marshall are concerned he has been, as my hon. friend knows, a provincial Minister of Agriculture, and has worked in connection with the federal Minister of Agriculture under a signed contract each year on the administration of his quota of the moneys to be expended under the Agricultural Instruction Act, and amounting probably in the case of his province to $75,000 per annum. Mr. Marshall knows, as few other men could possibly know, the weaknesses of that act. In this connection I think there is one very pronounced weak point in the statute and it is this: Although the statute is called the Agricultural Instruction Act and under its provisions
Supply-Agriculture

something' like a total of $10,000,000 is distributed, the distribution does not take into consideration the rural population at all but is made on the straight basis of population. That is one of the weak points emphasized by Mr. Duncan Marshall. I would therefore ask who should be better qualified to investigate the conditions of an act than the one who represents a province that has suffered under the past system of distribution. I am now opening up what may be a controversial question and I do not want to continue on that line-I would rather go ahead with my estimates. However I simply wished to demonstrate the facts and establish why we selected Duncan Marshall for this particular work.

I was
very much pleased to hear the minister state that Mr. Marshall's appointment was due to the fact that owing to pressure of public business at that time no men in the Civil Service were available. I am sure the minister will therefore be quite willing to give the committee the assurance that the appointment of Mr. Marshall to the position of Commissioner is merely temporary, and that as soon as possible one of the deserving members of the Civil Service will be promoted to fill it. If for no other reason than a desire to improve the morale of the service and to encourage the civil servants who are to work in conjunction and co-operation with him, he should now give us a guarantee that one of them will be appointed to the office as soon as possible.

If I can get the attention of the minister away from the subject of exhibitions I would ask him if it is the intention of his department to put into operation this season the Dairy Grading Act which was passed during the last session of Parliament.
I think my hon. friend refers to the Dairy Produce Act.
Will the minister please answer my question?

We were hoping to put the act into force the first of May so that by the time the rush of the season came on there would be as little disturbance as possible, but if so, matters will have to be greatly accelerated. The Civil Service Commission makes the necessar ' appointments and it may take them three or four months to do so-in fact I may not get the act into force at all for some time. Sometimes nearly a year elapses be-

fore they make appointments, so that when I speak of the date at which the act is likely to come into force I do so with that reservation in mind.
I see from the estimates that a new officer is being appointed as a " Canning Specialist." I would like to know what the duties of this new officer are?

That is an appointment made at the Experimental Farm. The position is vacant now but I understand it is to be occupied by a lady who will deal with the canning of fruits and vegetables and demonstrate the various processes.
I would like to know how many of the officers of the department are connected with the Experimental Farm in Ottawa?

Do you want a list of the employees at the Experimental Farm?
!Mr. CHAPLIN: I assume the minister is not going to get through with his estimates this evening, I would therefore like him to provide a list of the officers who are connected with the Central Experimental Farm. I think that is a question that relates to the civil list and I would like to discuss it. In my opinion that is one of the sources of great extravagance in Ottawa and if you want to put in the plug in the interests of economy that is a place where it ought to be done.
At the Experimental Farm?
Yes.
It would only lead the discussion very much afield if I went into that.
I asked the question.
There is the specific vote.
Can the hon. gentleman answer the question?
It would take a long time.

speechtext: Item 41 deals with the Experimental Farm, and will be found on page 92. It will come up later.

If this list goes
through, I will not get the information I want when I come to the Experimental Farms.
